records.name_note: NC State's dedicated Salvia x sylvestris page leads its prose with Wood Sage; its Common Name(s) list is alphabetized, Meadow Sage then Wood Sage, and its page-title parenthetical reads Meadow Sage, Wood Sage in the same order. The page's own text uses meadow sage for the parent S. pratensis and woodland sage for the parent S. nemorosa, so Wood Sage, the prose name, is landed rather than Meadow Sage and is kept distinct from Woodland Sage (a separate record). RHS's dedicated Salvia × sylvestris page title pairs the binomial with wood sage. NC State lists Salvia × degenii under Previously known as, and says it is not always possible to tell whether modern cultivars come from the hybrid or from unhybridized woodland sage.
unknowns: RHS has a dedicated page for the hybrid itself (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/97521/salvia-sylvestris/details), but it carries only the name, the common name wood sage and Botanical Details (Family Lamiaceae, Native to GB/Ireland No, the genus description, Name Status Correct); its Size section shows only Time to Maturity: No preference, and it has no sunlight, soil, pH or hardiness fields. RHS and Missouri Botanical Garden cultivar pages ('Mainacht', 'Rose Queen', 'Blauhügel', etc.) support nothing, and Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder lists only cultivars of this hybrid, so no RHS pH, hardiness or size data is used.

is_houseplant false: no admissible page frames this hybrid as a houseplant or describes indoor culture. NC State's Plant Type field lists Herbaceous Perennial and its USDA Plant Hardiness Zone field 4a-8b, and it places the plant in borders ('Use wood sage as an accent or mass planting in a border.'); its Landscape Location field also lists Container and Patio, outdoor placements.
toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: the NC State page states no toxicity, no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags.
is_edible left null: the page does not address eating; its 'fragrant leaves' tag is not a culinary claim.

soil_drainage moderate is read from the prose 'dry to medium moisture soils with good drainage and high organic content', with gravelly or sandy soils and drought only tolerated; the structured field lists Good Drainage and Occasionally Dry, which on their own would read drier.

water_regime left null: NC State gives only soil-moisture adjectives (dry to medium) and drought tolerance, and no watering statement; its flower description says rebloom occurs 'if moisture is available'.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State's page carries no pH field.
direct_sun_hours_max left null: the page says '6 or more hours' with no upper limit.

outdoor_sun_exposure is full_sun only, from NC State's structured Light field (its prose also says 'Plant wood sage in full sun'); RHS's dedicated Salvia × sylvestris page carries no sunlight field and cultivar pages were not used, so no other source adds values.
No temperature, humidity, indoor light, fertilizing or chill-damage figures on the NC State page; all left null. Hardiness zones 4a-8b are a survival rating, not a damage onset.

Size 18-24 in tall and 12-18 in wide is NC State's Dimensions block for the hybrid; the prose says it may grow as large as 2 feet high and 1.5 feet wide, and the stem description says stems can reach 30 inches. Cultivar sizes were not used.
NC State states it is not always possible to tell whether modern cultivars derive from the hybrid or from unhybridized woodland sage, so no cultivar content was used.

records.name_note: NC State's dedicated page for this hybrid is headed with the binomial Aquilegia x hybrida, written with an ASCII x and recorded here with the multiplication sign. Its Common Name(s) list reads Columbine hybrids, then Hybrid Columbines; the list is alphabetized, and the page-title parenthetical gives the same two names in the same order. The page's Description opens with the name Hybrid Columbines, and its singular, Hybrid Columbine, is used here. The same sentence says the plant results from a cross between A. vulgaris and A. canadensis, consistent with the hybrid sign in the binomial.
unknowns: Only one admissible source (NC State, plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/aquilegia-x-hybrida/) was used; no other admissible domain was searched for a dedicated page for this hybrid, and no parent-species page content was borrowed.
Toxicity: the NC State page prints no poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags, so toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null (no record, not a finding of safety).
is_edible is null: the page does not address eating.

is_houseplant false: NC State presents this hybrid only as a landscape perennial ('A great plant for woodland and shady gardens, naturalized areas, or cottage gardens.'), and its Landscape Location field lists Naturalized Area and Woodland; the page does not frame it as a houseplant or describe indoor culture.

water_regime is null: the page's only watering line is 'Provide irrigation during dry spells', alongside a soil preference for 'fertile moist but well-drained soils'. That is a soil preference plus an aside, not a watering cadence, so no enum value is assigned. Dry-down, check-depth and day-interval fields are null for an in-ground perennial.

soil_drainage is moderate from the page's 'fertile moist but well-drained soils' and its Soil Drainage tags Good Drainage plus Moist; this is a preference, not a fast-draining or consistently wet reading. Soil Texture tags list Clay and Loam (Silt).

outdoor_sun_exposure: structured Light tags are Deep shade (full_shade) and Partial Shade (part_shade); the prose says 'partial sun to full shade', which is why part_sun is included. The 'partial shade tolerant' tag is also present. direct_sun_hours_max is null because the only hour figures on the page are the site-wide light-category legend text.

Soil pH is not stated; temperature, humidity, light in foot-candles and fertilizer data are not on the page and are null. USDA zones 3a-8b are a hardiness range, not a chill-damage onset, so chill_damage_f is null.

Care lines as the page words them: 'Deadhead to prolong the bloom season and prevent self-seeding as they will not seed true.' and 'Cut foliage back if it becomes infected with leaf miners as it will grow back.' There is no schema field for these. Listed problems: leaf miner, stem borers, aphids, powdery mildew, leaf spots.

Size is from NC State's Dimensions block (Height 1 ft 0 in - 3 ft 0 in = 12-36 in; Width 1 ft 0 in - 1 ft 6 in = 12-18 in); the prose says 'grow 1 to 3 feet tall'. The page's Cultivars / Varieties entries read 'A. vulgaris' and are not used for any field.

records.name_note: Sources split on the primary common name. NC State's dedicated Heuchera americana page uses 'American alumroot' in its description prose, while its page-title parenthetical lists Alumroot first, then American Alumroot. RHS's page for this taxon is led by 'American alum root' (three words), and UMD Extension's dedicated page is titled 'Alumroot'. American Alumroot was chosen because it is the NC State prose name and appears in NC State's name list. NC State's list also carries Coral Bells and Rock Geranium for this species.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets, toxicity_detail and is_edible are null: the NC State page for H. americana carries no poison block and no cat/dog tags, and no admissible source reached names H. americana for toxicity or eating. NC State's line that the foliage is high in tannins and bitter and unappetizing to deer is a deer-resistance statement only. NC State's Ethnobotany line (roots contain alum, an astringent) is not an edibility statement.

MoBot (Heuchera americana, plantfinder.mobot.org / missouribotanicalgarden.org kempercode=k460) could not be fetched from this environment (connection error), so nothing was taken from it. No UF/IFAS, Clemson, PSU or UGA page dedicated to H. americana was found; the Clemson hit was a genus-level Heuchera page and was not used.

Light conflict: NC State's structured Light field lists Dappled Sunlight, Full sun and Partial Shade, with no Deep shade value, and RHS's Position field lists Full sun and Partial shade. NC State's own prose says 'Plant in moist, rich soils in shade to part sun.' and UMD's structured Sun field reads 'part sun to full shade; performs better with afternoon shade, especially in drier soils'. full_sun is left out because NC State's species prose and UMD's Sun field both exclude it. full_shade is left out because only UMD's Sun field names it: NC State's Light field stops at 'Dappled Sunlight (Shade through upper canopy all day)' and RHS's Position field stops at Partial shade. part_sun rests on NC State's prose and UMD's Sun field; part_shade on NC State's Dappled Sunlight and Partial Shade values, RHS's Partial shade and UMD's range.
direct_sun_hours_max is null: no species-specific prose gives an hour figure; NC State's 2-6 hour range is the site-wide light-category legend.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null: NC State's Soil pH is only the open-ended Acid (<6.0) band, and RHS pH says Neutral, so no closed range is supported.

water_regime is null: NC State gives only soil-drainage tags (Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Dry) plus a drought-tolerance trait, and RHS gives a Moisture soil descriptor (Moist but well-drained); no admissible source states a watering instruction. The 'moist, rich soils' phrase is a soil adjective.

soil_base garden_bed rests on NC State's siting sentence 'American alumroot is drought-tolerant and works well planted in small groups in the front of a border, along pathways, near a patio, in a woodland, rock, rain or shade garden.' and its instruction 'Plant in moist, rich soils in shade to part sun.'; NC State also lists Container under Landscape Location and tags it #container plant. No potting-mix source was found.

Size sources differ: NC State Dimensions give Height 12-36 in and Width 12-18 in (used); RHS Max Height and Max Spread are each 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in); UMD gives Height 1-2 feet. NC State was used as the anchor.

NC State says 'Cultivars are readily available, and it may be difficult to find the pure, wild-type species in the trade.' and that its three varieties 'are difficult to distinguish from one another', so nursery plants may be cultivars or hybrids.

No source states a chill-damage onset temperature, humidity, indoor temperature, fertilizer or watering-interval figures; these are null. NC State's USDA zones 4a-9b and RHS's H6 are hardiness ratings, not damage-onset temperatures.

is_houseplant false: no admissible source frames this as a houseplant or describes indoor culture. NC State's Plant Type field lists Herbaceous Perennial, Native Plant and Wildflower, its USDA zones run 4a-9b, and it sites the plant in borders, along pathways and in woodland, rock, rain or shade gardens; its Container location is outdoor container growing.

records.name_note: NC State's page for Athyrium niponicum has a Common Name(s) list of Black Lady Fern, Japanese Black Lady Fern, Japanese Painted Fern and Oriental Ladyfern (alphabetized; the page-title parenthetical gives the same four names in the same order), and its Description prose calls the plant the Japanese painted fern; common_name follows that prose name. RHS's species page uses the shorter 'painted fern' (page title 'Athyrium niponicum | painted fern'), and RHS marks Athyrium niponicum Name Status 'Correct' and lists Anisocampium niponicum among its Synonyms. The sources also split on var. pictum: NC State folds Athyrium niponicum 'Pictum' and Athyrium niponicum var. pictum into this species page under 'Previously known as', while RHS keeps a separate page for Athyrium niponicum var. pictum (page title 'Athyrium niponicum var. pictum | painted lady fern'). Only the species-level pages were used for data.
unknowns: No admissible source states toxicity to cats, dogs or humans for this species, so toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null.
No admissible source addresses eating this fern, so is_edible is null.

is_houseplant is false: NC State gives Plant Type Fern and Herbaceous Perennial and USDA zones 4a-9b and places it in in-ground settings; RHS's Patio and container plants suggestion is outdoor container growing. No admissible page describes indoor or houseplant culture. Temperature, humidity, indoor light, and chill damage are not stated, so those fields are null.

water_regime is null: NC State's moist, rich soil is a soil preference ('prefers') in Description prose, and RHS's 'Moist but well-drained' is a soil moisture field; neither is a watering statement. Fertilizing is not addressed by any source.
soil_ph is null: RHS lists pH as 'Neutral or Acid or Alkaline', so there is no usable floor or ceiling, and NC State gives no pH.

direct_sun_hours_max is null: NC State's species prose says it has the best color in light shade and excess sunlight washes out the color, but gives no hour figure; the hour ranges appear only in its Light tag definitions.

outdoor_sun_exposure is part_shade and full_shade. NC State's structured Light field lists Dappled Sunlight (Shade through upper canopy all day) and Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours), mapped to part_shade, and Deep shade (Less than 2 hours to no direct sunlight), mapped to full_shade; its Description prose says 'This plant prefers partial to full shade and moist, rich soil, with high organic content.' RHS's species-page Position field lists only Partial shade, and its Cultivation text says 'For best results grow in a moist but free draining soil in partial shade.', so RHS supports part_shade but does not list full shade; full_shade rests on NC State's Light field and its preference statement. No source warns against deep shade; NC State's 'Excess sunlight washes out the color.' is why no sun value is listed.

soil_drainage moderate rests on NC State's Good Drainage value (the only value in its Soil Drainage field) together with its prose saying the plant prefers moist, rich soil with high organic content, and on RHS's Moisture field 'Moist but well–drained' and Cultivation 'moist but free draining soil'. No source asks for consistently wet soil.

Mature size: NC State's Dimensions (Height and Width 1 ft. 6 in. - 2 ft. 0 in., i.e. 18-24 in.) is the anchor. RHS's species page gives Max Height and Max Spread of 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in.), which is smaller and disagrees; NC State was used because it is the structured dimensions block, and the RHS range is disclosed here.

soil_base garden_bed: NC State places it only in in-ground settings (Landscape Location: Pond, Rock Wall, Woodland; Landscape Theme: Rock Garden, Shade Garden; prose: 'It is a great addition as a front border plant in a shaded area, in a woodland area, near water, or in a shade or rock garden.'), and three of the four entries in RHS's Suggested planting locations and garden types list are in-ground (Cottage and informal garden, Underplanting of roses and shrubs, Flower borders and beds). RHS's list also includes Patio and container plants, but neither source names a potting mix, so garden_bed is kept.

Common name split: NC State lists four names alphabetized; RHS uses 'painted fern' for the species and 'painted lady fern' for var. pictum. No data were taken from cultivar pages such as 'Silver Falls' or from Athyrium filix-femina pages.

unknowns: MoBot's dedicated Hakonechloa macra page (https://plantfinder.mobot.org/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=285349) fails TLS from non-browser clients and was read at audit in a browser. MoBot's structured row reads 'Sun: Part shade' only, and its Culture note frames deeper shade as a tolerance ('Tolerates close to full shade, particularly in the hot summer climates of the deep South.'); full_shade is kept on NC State's Deep shade value, RHS's Full shade and NC State's 'It is an excellent plant for all shaded locations and is attractive when planted on slopes or sprawled over rocks.'

NC State's heat caveat beside its 5a to 9b zone field: 'It grows best in cool summer climates, and it may not tolerate the hot summers of the southern United States, such as zones 8 through 9.' NC State's variegated-form color advice is cultivar-specific and was not used for sun hours.

records.name_note: Sources split on the lead name. NC State's Common Name(s) field is alphabetized and begins with Common Torch Lily, and its page-title parenthetical lists the same five names in the same order; its Description prose calls the species Torch Lily and says it shares the common name Red Hot Poker with the genus. RHS's dedicated Kniphofia uvaria page gives red-hot poker as its common name: the subtitle rendered under its H1 reads red-hot poker, and its browser page title reads 'Kniphofia uvaria | red-hot poker'; its Other common names field gives flame flower. Red Hot Poker was recorded as the lead because it is the common name RHS's dedicated page gives, and NC State lists it among this species' names. RHS's synonyms include Kniphofia aloöides and the Tritoma names Tritoma burchellii, Tritoma recurva and Tritoma uvaria. Missouri Botanical Garden could not be read from this environment, so it did not contribute.
unknowns: Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder page for Kniphofia uvaria could not be fetched in this environment (host unreachable from the sandbox), so no MoBot citation was used and nothing was taken from it; its Size, Culture and Noteworthy Characteristics are unchecked.
toxic_to_pets, toxicity_detail and is_edible left null: NC State prints no poison block or edibility statement for this species and RHS carries none either.
water_regime left null: NC State gives only a soil adjective (medium moisture, Moist drainage tag) and RHS only a soil-moisture field, neither a watering statement.
water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_dry_down_target left null: no source frames watering for this in-ground perennial.

humidity, indoor light, temperature ranges, chill_damage_f and cool_rest_note left null: no admissible source states them; RHS's H5 rating and NC State's zones 5a-9b are survival ratings, not damage-onset temperatures.
direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's Light field is the structured category legend, no species-specific hour figure.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0) and Alkaline (>8.0), all open-ended or spanning, and RHS's pH field also accepts acid or alkaline or neutral.
Fertilizer fields left null: neither source gives a fertilizing schedule or strength.

Winter and crown protection (NC State): 'Torch Lily does not do well in cold winters and will benefit from mulch. Alternatively, you can tie the leaves together to form a canopy over the crown to prevent water from settling on the crown and freezing.' NC State also says: 'Site in an area protected from wind and cold and promptly remove spent flower spikes.'

NC State's Life Cycle field lists Bulb and Perennial, and its Tags row carries both #summer bulbs and #rhizomatous, while its Description says 'It can spread easily by means of rhizomes or seed.' NC State is split within its own page, so no bulb was recorded.

Size comes from RHS's structured Max Height 0.5-1 metres and Max Spread 1-1.5 metres (19.7-39.4 in and 39.4-59.1 in); NC State has no Dimensions block. The recorded height is RHS's Max Height band, not the height in flower, and both sources put the flowering plant above the band's 39.4 in top: RHS's own description on the same page reads 'An herbaceous perennial reaching approximately 120cm in height when in flower with green, linear strap-like leaves and spikes of tubular orange flowers that emerge from firey red buds in summer and autumn.' (about 47 in), and NC State reads 'It has a 2-foot-tall clump of 3 inch basel leaves and 4-foot-tall flower scapes with 10-inch drooping flowers that start red but turn to yellow in summer.' Expect flower spikes to about 4 ft above a foliage clump of about 2 ft.

NC State's soil prose says average to sandy, medium moisture, well-drained soils, prefers rich humusy soils, and will not tolerate wet, heavy soils; soil_drainage is moderate, not fast, and wet soils are a caution. Root rot in poorly-drained soils is noted.
Foliage habit differs: RHS says Evergreen, NC State's field says Semi-evergreen while its prose and tags say evergreen.

normalizations: 2026-10-09: b100 (popular garden perennials) landed from the post-audit records. Eight species: Wood Sage (Salvia × sylvestris) and Hybrid Columbine (Aquilegia × hybrida), both hybrids kept with the multiplication sign (NC State writes an ASCII x), American Alumroot, Japanese Painted Fern, Orpine, Wild Thyme, Japanese Forest Grass and Red Hot Poker. Auditor-supplied corrected wording used verbatim; every substitute quote was ground-truthed through verify_quotes' own fetch+extract path before it was applied. Landing decisions: American Alumroot's flagged sun list drops full_shade (UMD's Sun field alone named it; NC State's Light field and RHS's Position field stop at partial shade); seven null is_houseplant values land false on NC State's Plant Type and USDA zone fields (no Plant Type quote carries the next label, 'Woody Plant Leaf Characteristics'); Orpine's three NC State label-glued quotes (Soil Drainage, Soil pH, Attracts) trimmed to their values; Japanese Forest Grass gains a common_name citation (its prose-opener citation relabelled) and its RHS 'page title leads with' wording is corrected as the audit did for Orpine and Red Hot Poker; Wild Thyme's genus-level RHS bee sentence dropped for NC State's Attracts field. Missouri Botanical Garden refuses this machine, so none of the audit's optional MoBot citations was added; what the auditor read there in a browser is kept in unknowns and marked as such. No common-name collision with an already-landed record; no toxicity or edibility value was set (no cat/dog statement on any page).
